known.via: English Wikipedia "Ribera del Duero (DO)" (redirects to "Ribera del Duero")

communes: Montejo De La Vega De La Serrezuela

climate: Seasons this mild ripen Tempranillo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc fully without cooking off their freshness.
Tempranillo sits in its sweet spot, so the wines can show the style it is known for.
Garnacha is at its cool limit. In cool years it can stay underripe, with green, sharp flavors.

soil.rock: Gravel drains fast and is poor, so roots go deep for water and food. It holds little water.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 2°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Gentle slopes. Enough tilt to drain cold air and rain away, which lowers frost risk, yet still easy to farm by machine.

sheet.place: Ribera del Duero is a high plateau along the Duero river in northern Spain, at roughly 700 to 1,000 m. Summers are hot and nights are cold, so grapes ripen slowly and keep their freshness. Spring frost is a real risk. Locals call Tempranillo Tinto Fino or Tinta del País.
sheet.rules: A red must be at least 75 percent Tempranillo. Crianza needs 24 months of aging, Reserva 36 and Gran Reserva 60. At least 12 months in oak for the first two and 24 for Gran Reserva.

claims.claim: The first regulation of the Ribera del Duero denomination and its Consejo Regulador was approved by a Ministry of Agriculture order of 21 July 1982. The current regulation dates from an order of 1 December 1992.
The DO covers listed municipalities in four provinces: Burgos, Soria, Segovia and Valladolid, all in Castilla y Leon.

The vineyards sit on the Duero basin plateau. The pliego puts the valleys at an average of 750 to 850 m, with the high interfluve ridges reaching 1,014 m. Trade sources give about 700 to 1,000 m for the plateau, with most vineyards between roughly 760 and 945 m.
The climate is Mediterranean with a strongly continental character and some Atlantic influence. The pliego gives extremes of about 42 C maximum and minus 20 C minimum over the year.

During ripening the gap between day and night temperatures is usually 15 to 20 C. The pliego credits these swings, plus the high average altitude, for slow ripening, balanced acidity and softer tannins.
Frost is a real risk. The pliego gives the extreme frost-risk window as 17 September to 6 June. SevenFifty also calls frost a major threat and says it can strike from spring into early autumn.
Rainfall is moderate to low with dry summers. Aranda de Duero averages about 435 mm. The area gets more than 2,400 hours of sun a year.

The pliego describes the usual soils as sandy clays, ochre and reddish (Tertiary), plus middle and lower Duero terraces (Quaternary). The basin fill is mostly sands, silty or clayey sands, with layers of limestone, marl and chalky concretions. Soils are basic in pH and low in organic matter.

Gravel and pebble layers occur in places. A trade description of Finca Villacreces mentions sandy loam with layers of gravel and pebbles, and another survey puts clay with gravelly outcrops around La Horra and more limestone and chalk to the west.
Tinto Fino and Tinta del País are the local names for Tempranillo. The pliego lists them as accepted synonyms and names Tempranillo as the main variety for red wines.

Red wines must be at least 75 percent Tempranillo (Tinto Fino, Tinta del País). Other permitted varieties are Cabernet Sauvignon, Garnacha Tinta, Malbec, Merlot and, for whites, Albillo Mayor. Tempranillo is about 95 percent of plantings according to SevenFifty.

Red minimums under the pliego. Crianza: 24 months total, at least 12 in oak. Reserva: 36 months total, at least 12 in oak, the rest in bottle. Gran Reserva: 60 months total, at least 24 in oak, the rest in bottle.

Oak barrels for Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva can be at most 330 litres. The 'Roble' or 'Barrica' mention needs at least 3 months in barrel and allows up to 600 litres. Aging time cannot be counted before 1 October of the harvest year, and the count for the three terms starts when the wine goes into oak.
Rose and white minimums are lower: Crianza 18 months (6 in oak), Reserva 24 months (6 in oak), Gran Reserva 48 months (6 in oak).
The maximum yield is 7,000 kg of grapes per hectare (50.4 hl/ha) for all varieties except Albillo Mayor.

The wines are known for deep colour, a balanced natural acidity, firm yet high-quality tannin, power with elegance, and a strong ability to age. The pliego says aged wines are among the longest-lived in Spain. SevenFifty lists blackberry, plum, vanilla, spice, leather and tobacco as typical flavours.
Ribera del Duero holds DO status, not DOCa. SevenFifty says it was approved for DOCa in 2008 and did not pursue it.
Ribera del Duero means 'bank of the Duero', after the river that runs through the zone. The pliego refers to the Duero basin throughout.
